title: GA/50/2013 of State Of Uttarakhand Vs Jalendra AND ANOTHER

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
THE ACTING CHIEF JUSTICE SHRI SANJAYA KUMAR MISHRA
AND
JUSTICE SHRI RAMESH CHANDRA KHULBE
Government Appeal No.50 OF 2013

State of Uttarakhand ...... Appellant
Vs.
Jalendra & Another ...... Respondents
Counsel for the appellant : Mr. J. S. Virk, learned
 Deputy Advocate General
 along with Mr. Pankaj
 Joshi, learned Brief
 Holder for the State.
Counsel for respondent No.1 : Mr. Vikas Anand, learned
 counsel.
Counsel for respondent No.2 : Mr. Prem Kaushal, learned
 counsel.
Upon hearing the learned Counsel, the Court made the
following
Judgment: (Per Shri Justice Ramesh Chandra Khulbe)
This Government Appeal is preferred against the
judgment and order dated 16.03.2013 passed by 2nd
Additional Sessions Judge, Rudrapur, Udham Singh Nagar
in S.T. No.135/2008, "State Vs. Jalendra and another"
whereby the concerned Court acquitted respondent -
Jalendra under Section 376, 506 IPC and respondent-Urmila under Section 120B read with Section 376 IPC.
2. The brief facts leading to the case are that, PW1
Teju Ram Prajapati submitted an information Ex.Ka-1 with
Police Station, 17 Mile, Khatima, Udham Singh Nagar on
27.03.2008 with the allegations that Rajdev Maurya is his
neighbour where respondent-accused Jalendra S/o Sudama
1

R/o Village Haldi Bagh used to visit regularly and he had
made illicit relations with minor daughter of the informant.
This fact was revealed to the informant by his daughter,
who is four months' pregnant. Due to threat extended by
respondent-Jalendra this fact was not disclosed to anyone
by the daughter of the informant.
3. On the basis of the said information Chick FIR
Ex.Ka-3 was registered at Police Station Majhola, Khatima.
The statement of victim was recorded under Section 164
Cr.P.C. by the concerned Magistrate, which is Ex.Ka-2. She
was medically examined and the medical reports Ex.Ka-6
and Ex.Ka-7 are on record.
4. After completion of the investigation, charge
sheet Ex.Ka-11 was submitted. After compliance of
provision of Section 207 Cr.P.C., the case was committed to
the Court of Sessions. Accordingly, the trial Court after
taking cognizance framed the charges against respondent-Jalendra under Sections 376 and Section 506 IPC and also
framed charges under Section 120-B read with 376 IPC
against respondent-Urmila, to which they pleaded not guilty
and claimed to be tried.
5. To prove its case, the prosecution produced PW1
Teju Ram-informant, who stated that the respondent-Jalendra has made physical relations with his daughter due
to which his daughter became pregnant. Accused-Urmila
took the victim with accused-Jalendra. This fact was
narrated by the victim to the informant. Accordingly, he
submitted information with the Police Station.
6. PW2 is the victim, who stated that the incident
took place three years back. In my neighbour Urmila, who
is my friend, used to reside. Urmila had taken me and
introduced with Jalendra. I was unaware about Jalendra.
Urmila had taken me in a sugarcane field thrice. When I
met Jalendra for the first time, he offered me something to
2

eat on which I became unconscious. Jalendra raped me
against my will after removing my cloths. He raped me
three times on different dates. Due to this, I became four
months' pregnant.
7. PW3 Dinesh Chandra Upadhyaya stated that, on
the basis of information submitted by PW1 Teju Ram, the
Chick FIR was lodged at the Police Station, which is Ex.Ka-3
8. PW4 Dr. Sunita Chufal stated that on
28.03.2008, she was posted at CHC Khatima. She
conducted the medical examination of the victim. On the
basis of medical report, the age of the victim was found to
be more than 16 years and below 18 years and the victim
was 20-22 weeks' pregnant.
9. PW5 Ramesh Singh is the Investigating Officer,
who prepared the spot map and recorded statements of the
witnesses. After completion of the investigation, charge
sheet Ex.Ka-11 was submitted by him.
10. PW6 Dr. Lalit Singh stated that on 03.04.2008,
he conducted radiology of the victim. On the basis of
ultrasound, the victim was 20 weeks' pregnant.
11. After completion of the prosecution evidence,
the statements of respondents-accused were recorded
under Section 313 Cr.P.C. in which they denied all the
evidences. In defence, they did not produce any evidence.
12. After hearing learned counsel for both the
parties, the trial Court came to this conclusion that there is
no evidence against the respondents-accused and,
accordingly, acquitted the respondents-accused. Aggrieved
by it, the State Government preferred the present appeal.
13. We have heard learned counsel for both the
parties and perused the entire evidence on record.
14. As per the prosecution's story, the prosecutrix
was below 18 years of age at the time of offence. The
respondent-Jalendra committed rape with her on three
3

different dates. The victim was taken away by the
respondent-Urmila in a sugarcane field where Jalendra
committed rape with the prosecutrix.
15. As per the evidence, there is no documentary
evidence on record about the age of the victim. To
ascertain her age, she was medically examined.
16. As per statement of PW4 Dr. Sunita Chufal, the
prosecutrix was above 16 years of age. There is no other
evidence on record except the medical report.
17. Accordingly, we came to this conclusion that, as
per the medical report, the prosecutrix was more than 16
years of age at the time of the incident.
18. Now, coming to the conclusion, whether it was a
consensual sex or a rape? As per the evidence of the
prosecutrix, who appeared as PW2, accused-Urmila took
her at the sugarcane field where the respondent-Jalendra
committed rape with her. She stated that when she met
Jalendra for the first time, he offered her something to eat,
after which she became unconscious and the accused-Jalendra committed rape with her. She also stated that,
thereafter, she went again at the same place on two
different occasions where Jalendra again committed rape
with her.
19. So far as the offence under Section 120B read
with Section 376 IPC against respondent-Urmila is
concerned, the prosecutrix has clearly stated in her cross-examination that Urmila is residing with her husband at her
matrimonial home. She never came back at her parental
house after the marriage. There is no evidence against
respondent-Urmila that she took the prosecutrix to the
sugarcane field forcibly.
20. From the perusal of the statement of victim, it is
clear that the accused-Jalendra committed sexual act with
her on three different dates at the same place but the
4

prosecutrix did not disclose the date, time and even month
as to when the accused-Jalendra committed rape with her.
Even she did not disclose it to her father and other family
members although she was above 16 years of age.
21. So far as pregnancy of the prosecutrix is
concerned, the prosecutrix has stated that she gave birth to
a child but no DNA test was conducted by the Investigating
Agency to ascertain the paternity with respondent-Jalendra.
Presuming that, at the first time, some intoxicating
substance was given by the accused to her but after that
she again went at the same place to meet the accused-Jalendra which indicates that it was a consensual sex
between the prosecutrix and accused-Jalendra. During four
months' of pregnancy neither she made a complaint to her
father or other family members nor to Police.
22. So far as the statement recorded under Section
164 Cr.P.C. is concerned, she clearly stated in her cross-examination that she made such statement before the
Magistrate as per the instruction of Police, which shows that
as per the advice of the Police she gave such statement
recorded under Section 164 Cr.P.C.
23. In this connection, we take into consideration
the settled principle of law governing appeal against
acquittal as enunciated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in
the case of Ghurey Lal vs. State of U.P. reported in (2008)
10 SCC 450, wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court after
taking into consideration several earlier judgments
pronounced by it, has laid down following principles of law
while deciding the appeal against the judgment of
acquittal:-
"70. In light of the above, the High Court and
other appellate courts should follow the well
settled principles crystallized by number of
judgments if it is going to overrule or otherwise
disturb the trial court's acquittal:
5

1. The appellate court may only overrule or
otherwise disturb the trial court's acquittal if it
has "very substantial and compelling reasons"
for doing so.
A number of instances arise in which the
appellate court would have "very substantial and
compelling reasons" to discard the trial court's
decision. "Very substantial and compelling
reasons" exist when:
i) The trial court's conclusion with regard to
the facts is palpably wrong;
ii) The trial court's decision was based on an
erroneous view of law;
iii) The trial court's judgment is likely to
result in "grave miscarriage of justice";
iv) The entire approach of the trial court in
dealing with the evidence was patently
illegal;
v) The trial court's judgment was manifestly
unjust and unreasonable;
vi) The trial court has ignored the evidence
or misread the material evidence or has
ignored material documents like dying
declarations/ report of the ballistic expert,
etc.
vii) This list is intended to be illustrative, not
exhaustive.
2. The appellate court must always give
proper weight and consideration to the findings
of the trial court.
3. If two reasonable views can be reached -
one that leads to acquittal, the other to
conviction - the High Courts/appellate courts
must rule in favour of the accused."
24. It is trite law that the appellate court while
reassessing the evidence in a case wherein acquittal has
been recorded by the learned Trial Judge may come to a
different conclusion than the conclusion arrived at by the
learned Trial Judge but that shall not be a ground to allow
the appeal and set aside the acquittal leading to conviction
of the respondent. It is also trite law that the presumption
of innocence which is available to the accused persons at
6

the beginning of the trial it becomes reinforced by an order
of acquittal by the Trial Judge.
25. We have re-assessed the entire evidence on
record and reached to this conclusion that the prosecutrix
was above 16 years of age at the time of the incident. She
never made a complaint neither to her family members nor
to the Police during these four months of pregnancy period.
After first time of incident she again went to the same
place to meet respondent-Jalendra, which shows that it
was a consensual sex between the prosecutrix and the
accused which definitely does not come within the purview
of 'rape' as defined in Section 375 of IPC.
26. So, in this case, we are of the opinion that this
is not a case where the evidences have not been discussed
properly by the learned Sessions Judge or that he
committed material irregularity and perversity while
appreciating the evidence of the prosecution's witnesses.
So, in other words, we do not find any compelling and
substantial reasons to disturb the findings of acquittal of
the private respondents by the learned Trial Judge.
27. The prosecution has failed to produce clinching
evidence against the respondents. The trial Court has
rightly assessed the evidence and came to the conclusion
that there is no sufficient evidence to convict the
respondents-accused.
28. In view of the above discussion, we do not find
any infirmity or perversity in the impugned judgment.
Accordingly, the present Government Appeal is liable to be
dismissed and the same is dismissed.
29. Consequently, the impugned judgment and
order dated 16.03.2013 passed by 2nd Additional Sessions
Judge, Rudrapur, Udham Singh Nagar in S.T. No.
135/2008, "State Vs. Jalendra and another" acquitting
7

respondent - Jalendra under Section 376, 506 IPC and
respondent - Urmila under Section 120B read with Section
376 IPC, is hereby affirmed.
30. Let a copy of this judgment and order along with
the LCR be transmitted to the Court concerned for
compliance.

___
 SANJAYA KUMAR MISHRA, A.C.J.
 ___________________
 RAMESH CHANDRA KHULBE, J.
Dt.9TH JUNE 2022
